title: Certificates & Authentication
intro: Every component in the cluster authenticates with TLS certificates, and they expire. A node going NotReady out of nowhere, months after everything was working fine, is a classic symptom of an expired kubelet client certificate.

steps.prompt: Check how much longer the cluster's certificates have before they expire.
steps.fake_output:
CERTIFICATE                EXPIRES                  RESIDUAL TIME
apiserver                   Oct 15, 2026 10:00 UTC   17d
apiserver-kubelet-client     Oct 15, 2026 10:00 UTC   17d
front-proxy-client          Sep 28, 2026 10:00 UTC   1d
steps.explanation: kubeadm-managed certs default to a 1-year lifetime — 'front-proxy-client' with only 1 day left here is about to cause real problems if nobody acts.
steps.why: This is the single command that would have caught the incident before it happened — checking cert expiration proactively (e.g. via a scheduled job) is how real clusters avoid this becoming a 2am page.

steps.prompt: Renew all of the cluster's certificates before front-proxy-client expires.
steps.fake_output:
certs renewed for apiserver
certs renewed for apiserver-kubelet-client
certs renewed for front-proxy-client
(renewed 9 certificates)
steps.explanation: This renews every kubeadm-managed certificate in place, extending each by another full lifetime from today.
steps.why: You could renew just the one about to expire with 'kubeadm certs renew front-proxy-client', but renewing all of them together is the standard practice — it resets the whole cluster onto one consistent expiration schedule instead of tracking several different dates.

steps.prompt: The control plane static pods need to pick up the renewed certs. Restart them and confirm they came back healthy.
steps.fake_output:
NAME                             READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
kube-apiserver-master            1/1     Running   1          30s
kube-controller-manager-master   1/1     Running   1          30s
steps.explanation: Static pods pick up a manifest change automatically, but a plain cert renewal on disk doesn't change the manifest file itself — moving it out of /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ and back forces kubelet to recreate the pod and load the new certs.
steps.why: This is a slightly unintuitive step: the certs are already renewed on disk after step 2, but the running containers won't actually use them until they're restarted — the manifest move-out/move-back trick is the standard way to force that without an actual reboot.

steps.prompt: Confirm the renewal worked by checking expiration again.
steps.fake_output:
CERTIFICATE                EXPIRES                  RESIDUAL TIME
apiserver                   Sep 27, 2027 10:00 UTC   364d
front-proxy-client          Sep 27, 2027 10:00 UTC   364d
steps.explanation: Every certificate now shows roughly a full year of residual time again — the incident is resolved before it ever caused an outage.
steps.why: Checking again after the fix (not just assuming the renew command worked) is the same close-the-loop habit as confirming a rollout status or a pod's READY count after any other fix — never just trust that a fix command succeeded silently.
